acceptance_criteria.source: "Let's brainstorm about what in the codebase works alreacy, what's kinda there but needs some work to make optimally robust, and what's missing entirely and needs to be built from the ground up."
acceptance_criteria.text: The assistant audits the existing codebase (checkpointing, resume, Slurm/sweep tooling, data pipeline) and categorizes what already works, what needs hardening, and what is missing, before proposing a design.

acceptance_criteria.source: "1) appropriate checkpointing, both in terms of interval ..."
acceptance_criteria.text: The design addresses checkpoint interval/cadence appropriate for week-to-month runs with failures expected weekly or every few days.

acceptance_criteria.source: "making sure that we're actually saving everything we need to save at each checkpoint to rapidly perform a bitwise-clean resume"
acceptance_criteria.text: The design specifies the complete set of state each checkpoint must contain (at minimum model, optimizer, scheduler, RNG, training counters, data position) so that a resume reproduces the uninterrupted run as exactly as possible.

acceptance_criteria.source: "2) make sure we're managing everything correctly on the SUNK (CoreWeave's slurm on kubernetes) end so that resumes can happenen automatically on failures."
acceptance_criteria.text: The design covers how the Slurm/SUNK side is managed so that training resumes automatically after node/GPU failures.

acceptance_criteria.source: "so a 6-12B param model should fit pretty easily with a 8-16 batch per GPU, right?"
acceptance_criteria.text: The assistant answers whether a 6-12B parameter model fits on B200s (~180GB) at a per-GPU batch of 8-16, with reasoning.

acceptance_criteria.source: "i can envision trainijg somwthing in the 24-30B range as an absolute top end, so would you recommend planning for FSDP right from the jump?"
acceptance_criteria.text: The assistant gives a recommendation on whether to plan for FSDP from the start, accounting for the stated range of model sizes (6-12B now, up to ~24-30B), and the design reflects that recommendation.

acceptance_criteria.source: "will the autoresume behavior impair our ability to start a quick one-off training run on metal using oplm train (or more likely, accelerate launch -m oplm.train)?"
acceptance_criteria.text: The assistant answers whether auto-resume impairs quick one-off bare-metal runs via `oplm train` / `accelerate launch -m oplm.train`, and the design ensures such runs are not impaired.

acceptance_criteria.source: "nothing is going to be hard-coded for coreweave's infra, right? the idea is to release all of this as open source (training tooling included) so people can reuse"
acceptance_criteria.text: Nothing in the design or plan is hard-coded to CoreWeave's infrastructure; site-specific values are confined to user configuration so the tooling can be released as open source.

acceptance_criteria.source: "id also like `keep_every_n_steps` so that i can permanently keep checkpoints at every 100k steps or something"
acceptance_criteria.text: Checkpoint retention includes a `keep_every_n_steps` option (alongside the hours-based equivalent) for permanently keeping checkpoints at a step interval.

acceptance_criteria.source: "this, along with the `keep_every_n_hours` equivalent, should be immune from the save total limit, which is designed to cull the rolling checkpoints not eliminate those that are supposed to be permanently kept"
acceptance_criteria.text: Checkpoints matching `keep_every_n_steps` or `keep_every_n_hours` are exempt from `save_total_limit`, which only culls rolling checkpoints.

acceptance_criteria.source: "we should check the potential double-sharding issue and fix if necessary while we're in there"
acceptance_criteria.text: The plan includes verifying the suspected accelerate dataloader double-sharding issue and fixing it if real.

acceptance_criteria.source: "yes, write up the spec" — approving the design walked through section by section before turn 7
acceptance_criteria.text: A spec document is written into the repository (under the existing docs/superpowers/specs/ location) capturing the design the assistant presented and the user approved in turns 2 through 7, including the user's additions from turns 2-4.

acceptance_criteria.source: "Looks good, write out the implementation plan" — after the assistant stated the plan would go into TODOS.md per convention
acceptance_criteria.text: An implementation plan is written to TODOS.md (the repository's plan location the assistant named and the user accepted) and references the spec document.

acceptance_criteria.source: "write out the implementation plan" approving the plan as described; the phasing was presented before turn 7 and accepted with "yes, write up the spec"
acceptance_criteria.text: The implementation plan is divided into phases matching the phasing presented in the final design section and approved at turn 7.

analysis.task_statement: Brainstorm and then design fault-tolerant training for upcoming week-to-month runs on ~64 nodes / 512 B200 GPUs on CoreWeave SUNK (Slurm-on-Kubernetes): audit what the oplm codebase already has, what needs hardening, and what is missing for robust checkpointing (interval, completeness, bitwise-clean resume) and automatic resume on failure. After agreeing on an approach section by section, write the design up as a spec document in docs/superpowers/specs/ and then write a phase-divided implementation plan into TODOS.md, keeping everything portable (open-source release, nothing CoreWeave-specific hard-coded, one-off bare-metal `oplm train` runs unaffected).
